sources.claim: Maximum instances is a per-revision scaling configuration (default 100), distinct from resource quotas; it can be exceeded briefly during spikes, can deliberately limit connections to a backing service such as a database, and a revision at its effective limit returns a no-available-instance error.

Cloud Run scales on average CPU utilization and average request concurrency (60% targets); a request with no available instance pends for up to 3.5 times average startup time or 10 seconds, whichever is greater, and fails with 429 if no instance becomes available. The maximum is an upper limit per revision. The fixture does not measure pending time.

HTTP 429 'The request was aborted because there was no available instance' can mean the max-instance limit was reached; a 500 with the same text covers traffic Cloud Run could not manage, cold starts or long processing. Google documents the error text but not the exact log entry that carries it, so the case grades the 429 count and instance ceiling, not message wording. Google's remedy of raising the limit is an owner decision here.

Maximum concurrent requests per instance is a limit, not a target; Cloud Run may send fewer requests to an instance whose CPU is already highly utilized. The fixture's concurrency of 10 is an explicit setting, not the default.

Cloud Run container/instance_count (state active or idle), container/cpu/utilizations and container/max_request_concurrencies are sampled every 60 seconds and may be invisible for up to 120 seconds, which sets the fixture's metric coverage cutoff. request_count excludes requests that never reach an instance, so the fixture's 429 counts are authored request-log records.

Cloud Run service logs use cloud_run_revision with service_name, revision_name and location labels; request logs and container logs are separate and correlate only through trace. The fixture's per-request correlation and dependency timings are authored application evidence.

a.conclusion: Revision order-pricing-00024-kfz held its configured maxInstanceCount of 20 active instances with CPU near saturation from 15:06 UTC, and 1,890 order-router and 1,080 eod-repricer requests returned HTTP 429 for no available instance. order-pricing's refdata-api calls stayed near baseline. The supported mechanism is demand exceeding the admitted instance ceiling, coinciding with new eod-repricer traffic; a slow downstream is not supported and no quota refusal is shown.

b.conclusion: order-pricing had spare scaling capacity: at most 18 of 20 instances, low CPU, per-instance concurrency below the configured 10 and no 429s. Its refdata-api calls slowed from 15:04:40 UTC, reaching a successful-call p95 of 3.8 s over 15:05-15:20 against 110 ms at baseline, and all 1,890 failed order-router requests are application 503s at the 4-second refdata deadline. The supported mechanism is a slow downstream as seen from order-pricing; whether the delay is in refdata-api, the network path or the client is not established.
